# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–18 (Complete – Updated 137)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Summer of fifth year** (Chapter 18). Spring 1816 events completed. Winter 1815-16 passed. Waterloo campaign: 16 June 1815 morning—regiment receives marching orders; by dawn 17 June—wounded return; 18 June (Sunday)—religious services. **Critical event (26 March 1816)**: Rebecca delivers son (Rawdon minor) and heir to Rawdon. **Spring 1816**: Pitt marries Lady Jane at Brighton; moves into Miss Crawley's house. Lady Southdown assumes control. Miss Crawley dies (spring/early summer 1816). **Late autumn 1815**: Mr. Osborne announces trip to Belgium; church incident with George's monument; confrontation with Colonel Dobbin in Brussels. **Chapter 17 timeline**: Approximately 3-4 years after Paris establishment; Rawdon and Rebecca now in Curzon Street, May Fair, London. **Chapter 17-18 events**: Pitt receives Rebecca's letter (graciously); declines to send £30,000 to Rawdon but offers hand and willingness to serve young Rawdon; nearly reconciliation between brothers. Pitt and Lady Jane absent from London when Rebecca arrives; Miss Crawley's house in Park Lane not yet occupied; Miss Crawley's domestics dismissed with gratuities; French novels sold to bookseller on Bond Street. **Queen's Crawley visit (Chapter 18, new)**: Pitt and Lady Jane make formal visit to Sir Pitt after their marriage at family seat. Visit described as "awful and unfortunate," never to be thought of without horror. Pitt begged wife never to speak of it. **Seven-year period noted**: Journal-like account of Amelia's life for seven years after Georgy's birth would show few remarkable incidents beyond measles.
- **Queen's Crawley estate condition (Chapter 18, new)**: In state of ruin and utter dreariness. Park shows great gaps where old Baronet felling trees entirely without license. Drives ill-kept; great sweep and entrance stair black and covered with mosses; once trim flower-beds rank and weedy. Shutters up along almost whole line of house. Sir Pitt nearly eighty; afflicted with lumbago; does not attend respectable society; dislike for respectable society increased with age. **Final illness and death (Chapter 18, new)**: After evening of carousing with rum-and-water with Horrocks, Sir Pitt suffers sudden collapse. Boy on pony sent to Mudbury for Doctor. Mrs. Bute Crawley, Reverend Bute Crawley, and James Crawley immediately summoned; Mrs. Bute assumes command. Sir Pitt brought "back to a sort of life"; cannot speak but recognizes people. Mrs. Bute keeps vigil through night; Horrocks ordered away as "tipsy old wretch." Doctor present but sleeps. Reverend Bute and James consume additional rum. **Sir Pitt dies** (date unspecified in Chapter 18 passages, but clearly summer 1816). **Post-death observances**: All blinds pulled down at Hall and Rectory; church bell tolled; chancel hung in black. Family mourning observed; Bute Crawley avoids coursing meeting, dines quietly at Fuddleston. Family surgeon pays respects. Death discussed at Mudbury and Crawley Arms.
- **Locations**: London (Russell Square, Thames Street, Slaughters' Coffee-house, Gray's Inn Square, Hulker and Bullock bankers, Curzon Street May Fair, Fulham, Park Lane, Bond Street, Bayswater, Hyde Park, opera, Knightsbridge, nursery, parlour, ring), Brussels, Belgium, Waterloo battlefield, Brighton, Southampton, Paris, Faubourg St. Germain, Coldcombe hill farms, Dunholt, Calais, Dunkirk, Red Lion Square, Cursitor Street, Tooting, Gulton, Quenwick, Queen's Crawley, Clapham, Sugar-cane Lodge, Miremere, Valenciennes, Kensington Gardens, Hampshire, Madras, district chapel, tavern, Winchester Cathedral Close, Mudbury, Rectory, Parsonage, Hill farms of Mirecombe, Fuddleston, Southampton Gaol, Dunwick, Crawley Arms, Mudbury (saddler residence).

## Main Characters

**Sir Pitt Crawley (Baronet, elder) – DECEASED**
- **Status (Chapter 18, new)**: Elderly, afflicted with lumbago; does not attend respectable society; dislike for respectable society increased with age. Nearly eighty; wears well by his own assessment; attributes longevity to godliness, sobriety, moral life. **Reception of Pitt and Lady Jane visit**: Initial affection and crude behavior; pointed pipe, remarked Pitt had "got vat"; questioned if reads "very long zermons"; asked Lady Jane to "give old Pitt a kiss"; made crude remarks about her appearance versus his horse-godmother. Took snuff, leered at Lady Jane, pinched her hand. Said he glad she came; likes her face; expressed belief he shan't be here long. **Gift to Lady Jane**: Shuffled to cupboard, took old case containing jewels of value—pearls that belonged to his mother and afterwards first Lady Binkie. Thrust case into Lady Jane's hand. **Final evening (Chapter 18, new)**: Sir Pitt in great spirits; narrated Miss Horrocks' singing incident dozen times to Horrocks; thrummed on table; squalled in imitation; declared she ought to have singing-masters; drank extraordinary quantity of rum-and-water with butler Horrocks. **Collapse and death (Chapter 18, new)**: At very late hour, butler conducted master to bedroom. Half hour afterwards, great hurry and bustle in house; lights went about from window to window. Was brought "back to a sort of life"; could not speak but seemed to recognize people. **Final days (Chapter 18, new)**: Of sunshiny days, taken out in chair on terrace (Miss Crawley's chair from Brighton, transported with Lady Southdown's effects). Lady Jane walked by old man; evident favourite. He nodded to her, smiled at arrival, uttered inarticulate deprecatory moans when she left; cried and sobbed when door shut. Hester (maid) kind while lady present, but changed manner when alone—made faces, clenched fist, screamed "Hold your tongue, you stoopid old fool," twirled away his chair from fire. This all that remained "after more than seventy years of cunning, and struggling, and drinking, and scheming, and sin and selfishness--a whimpering old idiot put in and out of bed and cleaned and fed like a baby." **Death (Chapter 18, new)**: Dies during summer 1816. All blinds pulled down at Hall and Rectory; church bell tolled; chancel hung in black.

**Pitt Crawley (younger) – Now Sir Pitt, Baronet**
- **Status (Chapter 18, new)**: **Now Sir Pitt Crawley, Baronet**, with seat in Parliament; future honours in prospect. **Upon father's death, immediately plans**: "I'll clear the estate now with the ready money"; rapidly calculated its incumbrances and improvements. Will not use aunt's money previously lest Sir Pitt should recover and outlay be in vain. **Demeanor at father's death**: Pale face flushes quite red. **Post-death activities**: Avoids coursing meeting; dines quietly at Fuddleston with Bute Crawley, where they discuss deceased brother and young Sir Pitt over port.

**Colonel Rawdon Crawley**
- **Status (Chapter 18, continued)**: In London arranging inheritance affairs; wife and child followed; occupying furnished Curzon Street, May Fair house. **Character and relationships unchanged** from previous summary. Fond of Rebecca; she always perfectly good-humoured and kind; perhaps likes him better for being fool. He is her upper servant and maitre d'hotel. Has "great secret tenderness" for little Rawdon; takes him mornings to stables and park. **Park incident (Chapter 18, continued)**: Meets Corporal Clink with old gentleman and boy examining Waterloo medal. Gentleman says "He was a Captain in the --th regiment...Captain George Osborne, sir--perhaps you knew him. He died the death of a hero, sir, fighting against the Corsican tyrant." Rawdon blushes quite red, confirms: "I knew him very well, sir, and his wife, his dear little wife, sir--how is she?"

**Rebecca Sharp (Mrs. Rebecca Rawdon Crawley)**
- **Chapter 18 status (continued)**: Speedily became vogue among certain class; demeanor described in Chapter 17. Attends church regularly with Rawdon, carrying gilt prayer-books. **Toward son**: When little Rawdon cries overhead from garret, dismisses sardonically; tells Lord Steyne "he'll cry himself to sleep"; did not offer to visit child. **Scorn for husband**: Increases with his paternal tenderness (which doesn't escape her). **Social activities**: Displays herself at gatherings (fresh pink dress, dazzling white arms and shoulders, thin hazy scarf, curls round neck, prettiest little foot in sandal, finest silk stocking). Sings charming French songs, plays piano, charms with wit. **Encourages husband's absence**: Tells him "Don't stay and stupefy yourself at home to-night, my dear...Some men are coming who will only bore you...now I have a sheep-dog, I need not be afraid to be alone."

**Little Rawdon (Son)**
- **London period (Chapter 18, continued)**: **Hidden upstairs in garret or kitchen**, scarcely noticed by mother. Passed days with French bonne; when Frenchwoman departed, taken to housemaid's bed in garret by compassionate servant. **Relationship with father unchanged**: Rawdon affectionate and devoted; maintains private interviews every morning during shaving; sweetmeats hidden in old epaulet box. Father buys picture-books, walls covered with pictures father purchased and pasted. **Pony gift**: Little Lord Southdown bought black Shetland pony "not much bigger than a large rat." Father pleased to mount him and walk by side in park. Takes accustomed morning walks in park with father and pony.

**Mrs. Bute Crawley – Schemer and Controller**
- **Character (Chapter 18, new)**: Considers herself one of most virtuous women in England. Family presented to strangers as cheerful, loving, well-educated, simple. **Daughters**: Martha paints flowers exquisitely; Emma is "regular County Bulbul," verses in Hampshire Telegraph. Fanny and Matilda sing duets (Mamma playing piano; girls sitting with arms round each other's waists). **Reality (Chapter 18, new)**: Nobody sees poor girls "drumming at duets in private"; nobody sees Mamma drilling them rigidly hour after hour. She "put a good face against fortune and kept up appearances in the most virtuous manner." Got over yachting men from Southampton, parsons from Winchester, officers from barracks; tried to inveigle barristers. **Relationship with Sir Pitt (Chapter 18, new)**: Rupture complete; between Sir Pitt and whole county. Lodge-gates had not opened since Pitt's visit after marriage. Though good people of Parsonage shunned "horrid old dotard," kept strict knowledge of all happening at Hall. **Upon Sir Pitt's illness and death (Chapter 18, new)**: Immediately summoned; assumes command of everything; watches old Baronet through night. Never seems to want sleep; does not close fiery black eyes once, though Doctor snores. Calls Horrocks "tipsy old wretch"; bids him never show face again or be transported "like his abominable daughter." Sends express to Mr. Pitt Crawley (now Sir Pitt); keeps resolutely by bedside. **Regarding Miss Horrocks**: Seizes candle; orders Mrs. Brown to search Horrocks' room; tells Mr. Crawley (Reverend Bute) to go upstairs; assumes authority with calash and candle. **Post-death status (Chapter 18, new)**: Miss Horrocks leaves Hall when her father takes possession of Crawley Arms in village (leased from Sir Pitt); no visit to Southampton Gaol occurs. She and father leave Hall; ex-butler obtains small freehold, giving him vote for borough. Rector has another vote; these and four others form representative body returning two members for Queen's Crawley.

**Miss Betsy Horrocks**
- **Chapter 18 status (new)**: Found by Mrs. Bute trying at presses and escritoires with bunch of keys in Sir Pitt's study, wearing "guilty ribbons," with "wild air." Drops keys with scream of terror. Claims Sir Pitt gave her large pair of paste shoe-buckles "ever so long ago--the day after Mudbury fair"; pulls them from pocket, found in bookcases in study. **Hester's testimony (Chapter 18, new)**: Little kitchen-maid (late on promotion), Hester, denies Betsy's story; claims to be honest girl "though of pore parents and workhouse bred"; offers her own keys for search; swears never wrongly took lace or silk stocking. **Fate (Chapter 18, new)**: By time of post-death events, married to saddler at Mudbury; "cried a good deal" when death discussed. Good people of Parsonage were looking out for catastrophe as reward for her "immaculate love and virtue," but "Fate intervened enviously and prevented her from receiving" it.

**Horrocks (Butler)**
- **Chapter 18 status (new)**: Admits Pitt and Lady Jane; apologetically remarks "Sir Pitt ain't very well," hinting at lumbago. Later enters with salver and refreshments upon Sir Pitt's order. Attends evening of carousing with Sir Pitt; drinks "extraordinary quantity of rum-and-water" with master; at very late hour conducts Sir Pitt to bedroom. **Upon Sir Pitt's illness**: Makes "wild efforts" to assert authority and assist master; called "tipsy old wretch" by Mrs. Bute; bidden never show face again or be transported "like his abominable daughter." Terrified by her manner, slunk down to oak parlour. Ordered by Mr. James to get bottle of rum with clean glasses. Later, ordered to put down keys and never show face again. **Post-death status (Chapter 18, new)**: Obtains small freehold from Sir Pitt's property, giving him vote for borough. Eventually becomes landlord of Crawley Arms; becomes reconciled with Rector of late, who occasionally steps into parlour to taste "Mr. Horrocks' mild beer."

**Amelia Osborne, Georgy, Colonel Dobbin** – Status unchanged from previous summary.

**Hester (Little kitchen-maid)**
- **Chapter 18 status (new)**: Late on her promotion to greater household responsibilities. Defends herself against Betsy's accusations; speaks with humility of "pore parents and workhouse bred" origins; claims honesty; offers keys for search. **Later behavior**: While Lady Jane present with Sir Pitt, manner "always exceedingly bland and gentle"; changes when lady leaves. Makes faces at whimpering old fool; clenches fist; screams "Hold your tongue, you stoopid old fool"; twirls away his chair from fire; behavior cruel when unobserved.

**Reverend Bute Crawley**
- **Chapter 18 status (new)**: Summoned upon Sir Pitt's illness; arrives at Hall with wife and son James. Instructed by Mrs. Bute to go upstairs and ensure they're "not murdering your unfortunate brother." Joins Mr. James in oak parlour; tries bottle standing there; orders Horrocks to fetch another bottle of rum with clean glasses; sits drinking with Rector and son. **Post-death activities**: Avoids coursing meeting; dines quietly at Fuddleston with Bute Crawley, discussing deceased brother over port. Later occasionally known to step into Crawley Arms parlour and taste "Mr. Horrocks' mild beer."

**James Crawley (Reverend Bute's son)**
- **Chapter 18 status (new)**: Summoned with parents upon Sir Pitt's illness; arrives from Rectory. Orders Horrocks to get bottle of rum; sits drinking with Rector. Orders Horrocks to put down keys and never show face again.

## Critical Facts
- **Sir Pitt's death (Chapter 18, new)**: Dies during summer 1816 following sudden illness after evening of heavy drinking. Becomes "whimpering old idiot put in and out of bed and cleaned and fed like a baby" during final days. Dies with estate in ruin, trees felled without license, house deteriorating.
- **Pitt becomes Sir Pitt and Baronet (Chapter 18, new)**: Inherits title, seat in Parliament, prospect of future honours. Immediately plans to clear estate with ready money; will not use aunt's legacy previously lest father recover and outlay be in vain.
- **Miss Horrocks affair (Chapter 18, new)**: Caught by Mrs. Bute attempting to steal paste shoe-buckles from Sir Pitt's study. Claims Sir Pitt gave them to her. Denies by Hester. Later marries saddler at Mudbury. "Fate intervened enviously" preventing her expected reward for immaculate conduct.
- **Horrocks becomes landlord (Chapter 18, new)**: Obtains lease of Crawley Arms village pub from Sir Pitt; also obtains small freehold giving him vote for borough. Becomes partially reconciled with Rector.
- **Mrs. Bute's control (Chapter 18, new)**: Assumes complete command upon Sir Pitt's illness; maintains vigil; orchestrates household during crisis; takes charge of investigation into Horrocks' suspected theft. Demonstrates iron will and manipulation beneath facade of virtue.
